title: Silence is praise (Psalm 65:2)
hookLine: we can say what God is not better than what God is; "for Thee silence is praise"

cards: A prayer leader stands before the congregation, and he's on a roll. The prayer has three words for God: great, mighty, awesome. He keeps going.
Glorious, powerful, feared, strong, certain, honored. The list grows. In the room sits Rabbi Hanina, and he waits until the man is done.
Then he asks him, quietly: have you finished all the praises of your Master? The Talmud keeps that question, and Maimonides picks it up in the Guide.

teach.b: Silence is praise. First, the rabbi's point. Rabbi Hanina goes on: even the three words we say, we would not dare to say if Moses had not used them in the Torah and the sages had not set them in the prayer.
Then a parable. It's like a king who owns gold, and people praise him for owning silver. The praise isn't too much.
It's too small, and it insults. Second, Maimonides' turn. In the Guide he argues that any positive word for God, even a grand one, borrows from our own world and falls short.
What we can say more truly is what God is not. Not a body. Not limited.
Not weak, not ignorant, not made of parts. Each no, he says, brings you a little nearer, the way ruling out what something isn't sharpens what you know. Third, the verse.
In Hebrew, Psalm sixty-five begins its praise with the words l'kha dumiyah tehillah. Translations differ, and some English versions say praise waits for God.
Maimonides reads it: for You, silence is praise. Not silence as having nothing to say.
Silence as the right response once words run out. Fourth, the balance. He doesn't throw out prayer.
The fixed words stay, because the Torah and the sages gave them. What he warns against is piling on more, as if more words were more honor.
So the prayer is said, and then the silence after it says the rest.

how: In the Amidah, which is said quietly, those who pray it praise God as great, mighty and awesome, the words Rabbi Hanina defended. Students of the Guide study Maimonides' teaching on negative attributes in the chapters around 1:58–59.

o: a vow to stop speaking for one whole day
when words fall short, quiet becomes the truest praise
a rule that prayers may only be said silently

games.q: silence is praise — tap the pairs.
p: have you finished all the praises?

s: Maimonides tells people to stop praying the fixed words
the fixed words stay; he warns against piling on more.
in the parable, praising a king of gold for his silver is an insult
the praise isn't too much; it's too small.
every translation of Psalm 65 says 'silence is praise'
translations differ; some say praise waits for God. silence is Maimonides' reading.

games.q: you're Rabbi Hanina. a prayer leader keeps adding words of praise for God, longer and longer. what do you do?
o: join in and add a few more.
wait, then ask if he's finished all the praises.
games.why: he waits, then asks his question. even the three words we say, he explains, come only because Moses used them.

practice: If it fits your beliefs, say quietly one thing God is not, not a body, not small, and let each no stand by itself for a breath.
If God isn't part of how you see things, take something vast, the sea or the night sky, and say what it isn't: not a pond, not a ceiling. Then stop adding words, and let the quiet be there.

wordCard.voice: Silence is praise. Maimonides' reading of Psalm sixty-five: since we can say more truly what God is not than what God is, silence becomes a form of praise. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: silence, stillness. the word in Psalm 65 that Maimonides reads as 'silence is praise'.

carryVoice: Your line: silence is praise. Some things are honored best by stopping. See you tomorrow.
